newsitem.title: SPAIN: Controversial Spanish financier again delays trial.
newsitem.headline: Controversial Spanish financier again delays trial.

text.p: Jose Maria Ruiz-Mateos, one of Spain's most colourful and controversial financiers, once again put off his meeting with justice on Thursday by claiming illness on the day his long-delayed trial for business malpractice was to start.
Spain's high court decided to postpone for a week the trial of the former Rumasa SA chairman after hearing reports from prison doctors who said he had "symptoms of the flu".

In a case that has all the plot twists of a spy novel, the state had hoped to prove that he and seven other company directors falsified documents in order to deceive authorities on the financial health of his vast business empire.
Ruiz-Mateos, who once fled custody by donning a wig, faces up to 12 years in prison and having to pay, along with the other accused, 650 billion pesetas ($5.0 billion) in compensation.
The Rumasa case started nearly 14 years ago when the former Socialist government took over the holding company after it crashed spectacularly with losses of 300 billion pesetas.

At the time it was Spain's biggest business group by far with 20 banks and some 700 companies including hotels, insurance firms, the Dry Sack sherry producer and department store chain Galerias Preciados.

Ruiz-Mateos, 65, began his business career in 1961 with $3,000 and seven workers. By 1982, he had built Rumasa into a group representing almost four percent of Spain's gross domestic product and employing 65,000 people.
He still holds a deep sense of ownership for the former Rumasa, which the state broke up and sold off after the takeover, and a sense of injustice that he flaunts in regular publicity stunts.
He has variously appeared on the courthouse steps dressed as Superman, a bullfighter or a pirate.

In a characteristic gesture of bravado, Ruiz-Mateos refused to attend a pre-trial appearance last Thursday, forcing the High Court to order him into prison under the "extremely high probability he would flee".
He defiantly assured reporters even as he was being led away by police that he would not show up for what he called a "pantomime" trial.

"I will continue resisting by every means at my disposal until true, authentic and complete justice is given me and not this rudderless event that offends public sensibility," he wrote from his cell in a letter to newspaper El Mundo on Tuesday.
Ruiz-Mateos's exploits have at times defied belief.
He caused a sensation by putting on a wig in a bathroom during court hearings and fleeing to Germany where he was extradited in 1985 on charges of falsifying documents.
Under German law he could not be tried on the Spanish state's original charges of fraud, embezzlement and tax evasion and they were dropped.
He scuppered the first trial by firing his lawyer just as it was to begin, and further delayed it by getting elected to the European parliament in June 1989.

When his fellow European deputies voted to lift his immunity in February 1991, he appeared to have nowhere left to hide, but he appealed to the European court of Justice in Strasbourg and it ruled that Spanish justice had not given him a fair trial.

Most recently, the state prosecutor tried to get the case dropped because the charges are no longer criminal under Spain's new penal code, but attorney-general Juan Cesareo Ortiz ordered him to continue.
Unless his latest appeals work -- Ruiz-Mateos wrote letters to the queen and the prime minister asking for intervention -- he should finally appear in court on January 16.
